newsitem.title: USA: Dole steps up campaign pace, Clinton cruises.
newsitem.headline: Dole steps up campaign pace, Clinton cruises.

text.p: Republican Bob Dole announced on Thursday he would campaign non-stop for the last 96 hours of the U.S. election race in a herculean effort to prevent the re-election of President Bill Clinton.
"The last time I fought round the clock for my country was in 1945 in Italy," Dole said, recalling his military service in World War II when he was seriously wounded.
"I am determined to make every hour of this decisive election count," Dole said at a rally in Miami five days before the November 5 election. "The stakes are that high."

But the Dole campaign received a crushing blow from a new poll in California, which said Clinton had widened his lead from 10 to 18 points in the past two weeks -- even as Dole, in a costly and questionable strategy shift, threw himself into an effort to wrest the state away from Clinton.

He had decided to roll the dice in California after the earlier poll, figuring he could upset Clinton nationwide by stealing the state's 54 electoral votes, which are one-fifth of the 270 needed to win in the indirect U.S. system.

He poured $1.5 million a week into television spots and spent seven days in the state. In doing so, Dole pulled television advertising money out of other crucial states, virtually conceding them to Clinton.

"The campaign has crystallised. Clinton has a healthy double-digit lead and all signs are pointing to a fairly large Clinton lead," said Mark Di Camillo of the Field Poll, which conducted the California survey.

The same could be said nationally, despite the fact that Dole narrowed Clinton's lead to 7.7 percentage points in the latest Reuters poll. Reform Party candidate Ross Perot's support has been creeping towards the 10 percent mark in recent days.
A study of individual state polls by the Hotline political newsletter showed Clinton ahead in 35 states with 399 electoral votes. Dole led in 15 states with 135 votes.
Dole campaign spokesman Nelson Warfield said the 73-year-old Republican's final trip would be by bus, plane and other transport and would end in California.
He enlisted the help of former President George Bush, who appeared with him at a rally in Tampa, Florida, on Thursday.
"I believe in keeping the White House above partisan politics and away from these puny disputes we're seeing," Bush, who was beaten by Clinton in 1992, told the rally.

In accusing Clinton of running a partisan White House, Bush implicitly referred to brewing controversies over donations to the Democratic Party from people with ties to Indonesia, Taiwan and other foreign interests.
"Bob Dole is the person to lead this country into the next millenium. What it's about is leadership ... We need somebody to restore respect to America around the world," Bush said.
Clinton on Thursday focused on winning conservative-leaning Arizona, a feat no Democratic presidential candidate has managed since Harry Truman in 1948.
Revelling in his frontrunner status, the president also planned to criss-cross the country between now and next Tuesday making a final appeal for votes.
Aides said Clinton planned a major address in California on Friday on the issue of campaign finance reform in an effort to defuse that issue.
